key_finding: Shrouding the autopay-minimum option decreased minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, since nudged cardholders set autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards testing an autopay-shrouding nudge, with six-month outcome measurement.
why_it_matters: Shows that a choice-architecture nudge in a consumer financial product can shift a passive enrollment metric without improving the underlying financial outcome, and can even backfire for liquidity-constrained users — a direct warning against treating enrollment lift as the success metric.
limitations: Domain is credit-card repayment, not savings
No measurement beyond six months
relevance_reason: Directly tests a defaults/nudge intervention in a consumer financial app with liquidity-driven heterogeneity, closely analogous to the round-up savings design.

key_finding: Synthesizes plan-design research showing automatic enrollment and default investment options raise participation but can reduce longer-term participant engagement, moderated by financial literacy.
methodology: Narrative literature overview of defined-contribution plan design research. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides a recent, broad synthesis of default effects and their engagement costs that the team can use as a calibration point, even though the setting is employer retirement plans rather than a consumer app.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement setting, not consumer self-directed savings
Narrative rather than systematic review
No specific effect sizes given in abstract
relevance_reason: Recent broad synthesis of the exact default/engagement trade-off the brief asks about, useful for calibration despite domain mismatch.

key_finding: Argues that default enrollment in retirement plans induces behavioral inertia — low contribution rates, inactive account management, and account churn — such that participation-rate gains alone do not demonstrate welfare improvement.
methodology: Policy/opinion synthesis of existing empirical literature on default enrollment. Abstract-only, no original data.
why_it_matters: Directly restates the support team's objection — that passive enrollment produces disengaged, low-value participants — and proposes safeguards (auto-escalation, re-enrollment reminders) that transfer to a round-up design.
limitations: Employer retirement setting, not consumer app
No effect sizes provided, essay-style argument rather than empirical study
relevance_reason: Echoes and elaborates the internal counter-argument the brief explicitly wants evidence on.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how default choice-architecture effects persist or fade downstream, shaped by the time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience.
methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis of the default-effects literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the project a structured way to predict and measure whether the round-up default's enrollment effect will persist or decay, rather than assuming persistence by default.
limitations: Conceptual/theoretical, not an empirical estimate
Not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the persistence question with a general consumer-behavior framework applicable beyond employer plans.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive to the value of the default option.
methodology: Three natural experiments, including random assignment to default options, using Medicare Part D administrative data on low-income beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Provides some of the strongest available evidence that default effects persist over time and that inertia is not merely a short-run artifact — relevant to whether the round-up default's enrollment lift would be durable.
limitations: Health-insurance/drug-benefit setting, not a financial savings product
Population is Medicare beneficiaries, not general consumer-app users
relevance_reason: Strong quantified evidence on persistence and insensitivity of defaults, informing durability of enrollment gains despite a different domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and of default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, withdrawal at separation, and auto-escalation opt-out. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller once medium-run attrition and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: Retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
Focuses on job-separation dynamics specific to employer plans
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults durably raise saving, providing the counter-evidence the brief explicitly asked for.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment for low-income German employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted back out, with the default effect strongest when incentives were high and awareness of enrollment status was low.
methodology: Natural policy experiment using linked administrative and survey data on Germany's nationwide low-income pension auto-enrollment.
why_it_matters: Undermines the assumption that an opt-out default silently locks people in — a large share actively reverses it, and effect strength depends on incentive salience and awareness, directly relevant to whether an opt-out round-up default would be as sticky as assumed.
limitations: Public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer savings app
State as enrolling party rather than a self-directed digital product
relevance_reason: Quantifies how much of a default's headline enrolment effect survives active reconsideration, informing the persistence question.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains attenuate substantially between 12 and 36 months, though it still reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits this pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies how much of the enrollment/contribution gain from a default fades by medium-term horizons, speaking to the brief's core question about whether the effect persists at 6-12 months and beyond.
limitations: Retirement-plan setting rather than liquid consumer savings
Employer/national-system-mediated enrollment, not self-directed app
relevance_reason: Best available quantification of medium-term attenuation of default enrollment gains, central to the persistence question despite the retirement-plan setting.

key_finding: Default nudges produce medium-to-large effects on financial risk-taking, but recipients rate wealth-manager advice lower when a default is used (and lower still when they refuse it), an effect mediated by perceived advisor honesty.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative-sample experiment across five European countries (n=4207).
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial default reads as manipulative versus helpful in a consumer-facing EU context — the exact reputational risk the brief flags — and argues for individualized defaults over one-size-fits-all, bearing directly on both the entry and level design decisions.
limitations: Wealth-management advice setting rather than a mobile banking app
No long-term persistence data
relevance_reason: Directly quantifies the reputational/manipulation cost of defaults in an EU consumer financial-advice setting, the closest evidence to the brief's dark-pattern concern.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the default contribution rate and default fund, and half still did so after three years — clear anchoring on the default.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms on 401(k) automatic enrollment, tracked over several years.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration of anchoring on preset default levels that all subsequent 'does the preset level distort choice' work argues with — sets the baseline the pre-set multiplier decision should be measured against.
limitations: Employer 401(k) setting rather than a consumer app
Predates modern digital/liquid-savings and EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: The classic evidence for anchoring on a preset default level, directly relevant to whether a pre-set round-up multiplier will anchor choice.

key_finding: Default adherence decomposes into deviation cost and opt-out cost, both jointly necessary (84% of adherence from their interaction); adding an intermediate 15% preset tip option below the existing menu captures 69% of achievable welfare gain at only 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping transactions, validated against a stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Gives a rigorous, quantified account of how much of a default's grip on behavior is preference-driven versus friction-driven, and shows empirically how changing a menu of preset levels reallocates behavior and welfare — directly informs the preset multiplier design decision.
limitations: Domain is tipping, not savings or financial products
Single-shot decision rather than a recurring enrollment/contribution choice
relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative evidence on how changing a preset menu of default levels shifts consumer choice and welfare, directly analogous to the round-up multiplier decision.

key_finding: Under an opt-in payroll-deduction design for a liquid, withdrawable short-term savings product, take-up was very low (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees), but of those who opted in, 96% still held a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution 12 months later.
methodology: Field study following employees at five UK firms after introduction of an opt-in short-term savings payroll-deduction program, up to 12 months post-activation.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the opt-in trade-off for a liquid, withdrawable savings product much like the round-up pot: strong persistence among those who choose in, but near-negligible enrollment without a stronger nudge — a key data point for weighing opt-in against opt-out/active-choice.
limitations: Employer payroll-mediated program rather than a standalone consumer banking app
Small number of firms (five), UK only
relevance_reason: The closest available evidence on enrollment and 12-month persistence for a short-term liquid savings product under an opt-in design, directly bearing on the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: Only about 15% of individuals are 'active savers' who respond to tax subsidies (each $1 of subsidy raises total saving by roughly 1 cent due to crowd-out), while 85% are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but strongly moved by automatic employer contributions.
methodology: Population-level administrative panel data (41 million observations) from Denmark, comparing active-choice subsidy responses to automatic/default contribution changes.
why_it_matters: The foundational large-scale demonstration that passive savers vastly outnumber active choosers and are only moved by automatic (default) contributions, a key data point on whether active choice alone can substitute for a default in mobilizing most users.
limitations: Danish retirement/taxable-account system, not a consumer savings app
Pre-dates recent liquid-savings and EU dark-pattern regulatory concerns
relevance_reason: Landmark evidence on the size of the passive-saver majority and their unresponsiveness to active-choice-style incentives, foundational to the entry-mechanism debate the brief poses.

key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — a forced-choice design that highlights losses in the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic (opt-out) enrollment when defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a novel loss-framed variant against standard opt-out/default designs; abstract-only detail on effect sizes.
why_it_matters: This is the clearest test of exactly the 'active choice' option the brief is deciding between for feature entry, and its enhanced variant (highlighting the loss from not saving) is a directly buildable onboarding-screen design for the round-up feature.
limitations: conducted in medication-adherence field experiments, not a consumer financial product
no persistence/6-month outcome data given
abstract does not quantify effect sizes
relevance_reason: Directly proposes and tests the active-choice/enhanced-active-choice mechanism that is one of the three entry options the brief is choosing between, with an explicit note that opt-out policies originated in savings behavior.

key_finding: A synthesis of household finance behavior and the interventions (education, peer effects, product design, choice architecture, disclosure, and direct price/quantity mandates) used to shape it, contrasted against the standard classical model.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter covering consumption-savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance; abstract-only, no primary data or effect sizes given.
why_it_matters: Provides the broad behavioral-economics backdrop against which choice-architecture tools like defaults and active choice sit, useful context for framing the trade-off between enrollment lift and engagement, though not specific to round-up savings design.
limitations: household finance broadly, not focused on liquid consumer savings apps
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes for defaults specifically
does not isolate active-choice vs opt-out comparisons
relevance_reason: Serves as a general review of behavioral household-finance interventions including choice architecture, offering background on where default effects sit within the wider toolkit, but too general to directly settle the entry or level decisions.
